newsitem.title: USA: Freighter still stuck in Florida marine sanctuary.
newsitem.headline: Freighter still stuck in Florida marine sanctuary.

text.p: Salvage workers tried Tuesday to stabilise a container ship stuck on a shoal in a Florida marine sanctuary as the U.S. Coast Guard investigated a six-hour delay in reporting the grounding.

The 600-foot (200-metre) Liberian-flagged Contship Houston wandered off course Monday enroute from New Orleans to Valencia, Spain, and ploughed into an area of sand and delicate coral reefs in the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary about 12 miles (19 km) southeast of Key West.

The shoal is well inside a shipping exclusion zone closed to vessels larger than 155 feet (50 metres), officials said. The freighter, carrying general cargo and 800,000 gallons (3 million litres) of fuel, was aground in an area of water ranging in depth from about seven feet to 30 feet (two to nine metres).
The ship's crew did not report the accident until nearly six hours after the vessel ran aground, U.S. Coast Guard spokesman Charles Smith said.
"They ran aground at 11:45 p.m. Sunday. They called us on the third (Monday) at 5:30 a.m.," Smith said. "By not contacting us immediately, they broke the law."
He said the delay had emerged through interviews with crew and investigators were trying to determine why it took so long for the captain to report the accident.

Authorities said none of the fuel had leaked but the ship had caused damage to the coral, which covers about 20 percent of the bottom in the area. Salvors planned to pump in ballast water to keep the ship from moving and causing further damage to the reef, Smith said. Rolling or shifting of the ship would pulverize delicate corals.
"It's pretty hard aground, but I guess it has shifted a little bit," Smith said. "The most important thing is no more damage to the environment."

He said the owner of the vessel, Transportacion Maritima Mexicana of Mexico, had hired a salvage company but its salvage plan still had to be approved by the Coast Guard before an attempt could be made to refloat the ship.

The Houston ran aground less than a week after Florida's governor and Cabinet gave approval to the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary, which was first proposed after a series of ship groundings off the Keys in 1989.

The sanctuary harbours the only living coral reef in North America, a tract that has been severely damaged during the past two decades by pollution, overdevelopment in the Keys and careless boaters and divers. Corals grow at a rate of only a couple of inches (5 cm) or less per year and damage caused by ships can take decades to regenerate.
